Fulpati Ceremony, 2001 (2058 B.S.): His Majesty King Gyanendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev attending the Fulpati ceremony for the first time following His accession to the Throne in 2001, accompanied by Her Majesty Queen Komal Rajya Lakshmi Devi Shah and Their Royal Highnesses, then Prince Paras Bir Bikram Shah Dev and then Princess Himani Rajya Lakshmi Devi Shah. Fulpati, celebrated on the seventh day of Bada Dashain, is one of Nepal’s most significant religious and cultural traditions. The word Fulpati literally means “flowers and leaves” and refers to an auspicious collection of sacred plants, including Jamara, banana stalks and sugarcane, offered in worship to Goddess Durga. Historically, the royal Fulpati procession carried these sacred offerings from Gorkha, the ancestral seat of the Shah dynasty, to Hanuman Dhoka Durbar in Kathmandu. Accompanied by priests, traditional musical ensembles and the Royal Nepalese Army, the procession symbolised the continuity of Nepal’s religious heritage and royal traditions. During the monarchy, the King and the Royal Family participated in the ceremony, which was marked by elaborate military honours at Tundikhel before the sacred offerings were installed at the royal palace.
